newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Armed gangs terrorise southern Albania.
newsitem.headline: Armed gangs terrorise southern Albania.

text.p: Armed gangs roamed at will through rebel-held towns in southern Albania on Wednesday robbing motorists, terrorising women and shooting at travellers from Greece.

A rebel council running the port of Sarande said anyone caught stealing or looting would be shot, but such warnings had little affect on gangs, often well armed, operating mostly on the outskirts of the town where there were no rebel patrols.

"I fear that the real war will start now," said Fetisi Mercuri, the owner of a small cafe. "I take all valuables at night and have hired one man with a Kalashinikov to guard my shop. They have tried to break in two times in the past week."

About 2,000 inmates, most of them convicted of murder, rape, theft and drug deals, have escaped from prisons across southern Albania in the past 10 days. An estimated 150,000 assault rifles were looted from army barracks.
"These criminals all have Kalashnikovs now," said Aristide Hoxha, who runs a small hotel. "They'll kill you for a dollar."

Witnesses said an Albanian merchant was shot on Tuesday by masked youths controlling an abandoned Albanian customs post at the Kakavia border crossing with Greece. He had refused to hand over his money.

"He was shot in the stomach. He just layed there in a pool of blood a few metres (yards) from the border. Those who shot him fled in an open small truck," taxi driver Vangel Sourouti said. "I was very frightened and rushed off."
The victim, Musati Figiri, 31, died a few hours later in a hospital in the northern Greek city of Ioannina.

Foreign reporters in the area have been stopped at gunpoint by stranded drivers looking for petrol. Medical aid groups put on hold the delivery from Greece of surgical and medical supplies after a six-member gang tried to raid Sarande's hospital early on Wednesday.
Such gangs are largely outside the reach of rebel guards and could put up a good fight if confronted. With the collapse of the military and police in the south, much of the region is at their mercy.
The Greek consul in Gjirokaster has received scores of calls from members of the large Greek minority in the south whose shops and houses have been raided.

Sarande's streets empty long before the start of a night curfew imposed by the rebel council. Shots from automatic weapons often break into the night's nervous silence. A rebel patrol on Wednesday chased off three masked gunmen near a hotel used by foreign reporters.

Unconfirmed reports said women had been raped outside Sarande and some journalists have crossed at Kakavia under protection of armed rebels. The abandoned customs building in Kakavia was looted on Tuesday.

"They broke all the windows and took everything from inside. Furniture, doors, telephones, uniforms and state documents," said witness Mustafa Hasari. "They worked for hours, put everything on old army trucks and headed north."

An abandoned eight-storey state hotel was looted and set on fire in Sarande on Tuesday. Milk and flour are running out as truck drivers fear to cross from Kakavia and Sarande's only supplies arrive in small boats from the Greek island of Corfu.
